sentences: This is a square painting, just 45 centimetres on each side, smaller than many people expect.
The Dutch painter Piet Mondrian made it in Paris in 1930, and today it belongs to the Kunsthaus Zürich in Switzerland.
Mondrian stripped away every trace of nature to show a universal harmony with line and primary colour alone.
He called this approach Neo-Plasticism.
In his pictures, no curves or diagonals remain, only the vertical and the horizontal.
First, follow the black lines.
Verticals and horizontals divide the surface into a grid, yet their thickness varies slightly, and you can still see the marks of the brush.
These lines were drawn by hand, not by a machine.
The large red square filling the upper right is the star of the picture, covering almost half the surface.
It runs right to the top and right edges of the canvas, as if it might continue beyond the frame.
Down at the lower left sits a blue rectangle.
It is much smaller than the red, but its deep, cool colour holds the eye firmly.
Along its bottom edge is a tiny signature, PM 30: the painter's initials and the year 1930.
The broad white area along the bottom is not simply empty.
For Mondrian, white was a plane in its own right, and here it gives the colours room to breathe.
The white areas differ in size, too, and they set the rhythm of the surface just as much as the colours do.
Now the far lower right corner.
The smallest colour, a yellow, is tucked in between black lines.
Together with the blue at the left and the red above, this little yellow shares the weight and completes the balance.
There is no symmetry anywhere, yet nothing wobbles, because the size of each area and the weight of each colour are tuned so precisely.
Here, balance comes from the relationships between unequal parts, not from mirror images.
The painting was made at the request of the Zurich architect Alfred Roth.
On the back, dated Paris, January 1930, Mondrian wrote a dedication to his friend about seeking relationships and balance as a way of preparing the future.
Roth gave the work to the Kunsthaus Zürich in 1987.
Mondrian later repeated this composition several times.
Each time he enlarged the canvas by five centimetres, while keeping the black lines exactly the same width.
An experiment that began on this small canvas slowly grew.
Step back and look at the whole once more.
A few lines, three primary colours and some white are all there is.
If you took away just one colour, what would happen to this taut balance?
